lesson.title: When the Line Runs Out of Evidence
lesson.summary: Extrapolation, using a regression equation to predict far outside the range of observed x-values, can produce confident looking numbers that have no real support in the data.
lesson.body:
Extrapolation means using a regression equation to predict a response for a value of the explanatory variable that falls outside the range actually observed in the data used to build the line. It is mechanically identical to any other prediction, the exact same substitution into y-hat equals b0 plus b1 times x, but the trust that substitution deserves changes completely the moment x leaves the observed range of the original data.

The danger is that the least squares line was fit, and its linear form was validated, only by looking at the scatterplot across the span of x-values that were actually collected. There is no evidence, and absolutely no guarantee, that a real relationship continues in a straight line forever in either direction. Relationships in the real world routinely bend, flatten out, level off, or even reverse direction outside the window where they were originally measured, and a straight line has no way of knowing that, since it was built purely to minimize squared error within the data it was actually given.

Return to the worked example, where hours studied ranged only from 1 to 5 and the equation was predicted score equals 39 plus 10 times hours studied. Suppose someone plugs in 20 hours studied, far outside that observed range. The equation returns 39 plus 10 times 20, which is 39 plus 200, equal to 239. Since most exams are scored out of 100 points, a predicted score of 239 is not just uncertain, it is flatly impossible, a clear signal that the line has been pushed into territory it was never actually built or tested to describe.

The intercept discussed in an earlier chapter is itself a milder example of the same underlying problem: predicting for 0 hours studied, also outside the observed range of 1 to 5, returned 39, a number that carried real uncertainty precisely because it was never tested by any actual data point in the original study.

This kind of failure is not unique to exam scores. A regression line fit to a child's height between ages 2 and 10 will show a strong, believable, roughly linear growth trend across those years, but extending that same line out to age 40 would predict a height of many feet, since real human growth slows and eventually stops in ways a straight line has no way to represent. The arithmetic of extrapolation is always the same simple substitution, but the real world process being modeled is under no obligation to keep behaving in a straight line once the evidence runs out.

The practical safeguard is simple and should be applied before reporting any prediction to anyone: check whether the x-value used falls inside the range of the original data. If it does, the prediction is interpolation and can generally be reported with reasonable confidence, provided the linear fit was strong to begin with. If it falls outside that range, the prediction is extrapolation, and it should be treated with real skepticism, clearly flagged as such, or avoided entirely, no matter how confident and precise the equation looks once the numbers are simply plugged in.
